newsitem.title: UK: Brazil euro-linked bond innovative but sales slow.
newsitem.headline: Brazil euro-linked bond innovative but sales slow.

text.p: Brazil became the first emerging market borrower on Monday to launch a bond tailored to take into account the likely advent of a European single currency in 1999.
The parallel bond -- so-called because it consists of three simultaneously launched tranches in Austrian schillings, Dutch guilders and French francs -- was praised as innovative and ground-breaking.
But dealers said it was taking investors a while to absorb the new structure from a non-investment grade borrower which slowed first day sales of the $540 million equivalent bond.

"The bond was never intended to be a blow-out, but within the parameters which we had fixed we have sold twice as much to institutions than we predicted on day one," an official at underwriter ING Barings said.
The buyers' need to get approval to purchase a lower-rated bond also inhibited sales, but the general lack of high-yielding paper is expected to boost demand this week, bankers said.
Brazil is rated BB-minus by Standard and Poor's Corp and B1 by Moody's Investors Service.
Although some syndicate officials called the parallel structure "gimmicky", Argentina and Mexico are mooted to follow suit.
Brazil's bond opened up three new currency sectors for the country and is expected to pave the way for other Brazilian entities. It also broadened Brazil's pan-European investor base.

Some traders said they would have preferred to see an established currency such as the mark tapped, where Brazil has issued before and where its name is well known. But underwriters said a mark tranche may have caused an imbalance and arbitrage between the tranches.
ING Barings syndicate manager said the parallel structure was a creative marketing angle which also enabled Brazil to secure more defined geographical placement.
"Geographical placement will be blurred by the single currency while today Brazil can build their name inside these countries," he said.
Paribas syndicate manager said the structure boosted sales as some institutional investors were able to buy more paper due to its euro-fungibility clause in an otherwise defensive market.
All tranches have the same five-year maturity and pay a 6.625 percent coupon which will be fungible after EMU, creating a more easily tradable euro-Eurobond.
This year a number of borrowers have launched parallel bonds to position themselves with investors ahead of EMU, but so far this has been restricted to European investment-grade borrowers.
Joint lead managers ING Barings, Banque Paribas and Creditanstalt-Bankverein, said the pricing was based on outstanding trading levels of similar Brazil debt.
The Austrian schilling tranche yields 6.65 percent, the Dutch guilder tranche yields 6.613 percent and the French franc tranche yields 6.75 percent. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7718
